paper_title: Procedura: Agentic 3D Modeling with Procedural Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Native 3D generators now recover impressive mesh geometry from a single image. However, a dense mesh stays soft where a machined object should be sharp, it carries no part decomposition, and it exposes no parameter a user could edit. To address this, we explore the paradigm of 3D shape as code, leveraging and scaling the coding ability of an LLM for 3D modeling. We introduce Procedura, a novel 3D modeling agent framework that writes an object as a procedural assembly, a parametric program whose named parts are joined by typed, machine-checkable mates. From a text prompt, the agent plans the object as an assembly graph and writes the program part by part, solving each placement from the mated frames rather than guessing it, and admitting a part only once compile, mate, and connectivity checks pass. A decoupled vision critic then refines the assembly one diagnosed fix at a time. Moreover, the same graph carries per-part materials and a simulator-validated articulation. We evaluate on P3D-Bench under its assembly judge, and with the same judge on MechBench-36, our hard-surface benchmark. On both, Procedura outperforms state-of-the-art native 3D generators and every prior 3D-code agent on judged quality, produces the sharpest edges of any method we evaluate, and is the only one whose output is an editable, part-structured program.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Machines, vehicles, and tools are the objects that fill games, simulators, and factory floors, and generating them is fundamental problem at the intersection of computer vision and graphics. Native 3D generators have advanced rapidly and now recover impressive mesh geometry from single image [15, 37, 42, 46]. However, neither of the two dominant generator families turns this fidelity into usable production asset. Native generators produce the shape as an SDF or voxel grid, whereas autoregressive generators write the mesh directly, vertex by vertex and face by face [5, 27, 35]. Both are trained on large 3D datasets that are hard to collect, and both output raw triangles with no structure attached. Neither family delivers geometry that is both detailed and precise. Surfaces decoded from grid stay soft and scan-like where machined object demands sharp edges and exact faces, and meshes written token by token hold only as much detail as the token budget allows. Nothing in the mesh says which triangles belong to which part. part decomposition must therefore come from separate segmentation model applied afterwards [24, 50, 51], and even then the cuts follow surface geometry rather than meaning, so we still cannot reliably tell which piece is, say, the left finger of robot hand. Editing is also hard, since the mesh exposes no parameter to adjust; changing the object means sculpting the surface directly, which shuts out the non-expert user. Taken together, prior methods fall short on high-precision geometry, meaningful part decomposition, and editability. Writing the shape as code offers another route, since program is parametric and part-structured by construction. State-of-the-art LLMs such as GPT and Gemini [9, 29] now write high-quality code, and this ability already reaches 3D, from Three.js scenes to Blender scripts [12, 26]. Yet 3D shape that an LLM writes as code still comes out toy-like, extremely low-poly and without fine detail [48]. The gap has cause. single pass must commit every part, dimension, and placement at once, with no view of what its code builds. Even 2 Figure 3. Overview of Procedura. From text prompt, Procedura first synthesizes reference view and then runs three stages. In Planning, it decomposes the object into an assembly graph of named parts joined by typed mates. In Procedural Modeling, the mate-driven build, it writes the 3D program part by part; each part is generated against its mates and render of the partial build, its placement is solved from the mated frames, and verification stack of compile, mate, and connectivity checks guards every commit. In Refine, decoupled vision critic diagnoses the rendered model and gates one fix at time. The same graph then completes the asset with per-part materials and an articulation validated in Isaac Sim. recent agentic systems do not close this gap [1, 7, 55]. Can we use the coding ability of an LLM to generate detailed, high-quality 3D shapes that meet the three requirements above? To answer this question, we design Procedura  (Fig. 1)  , an agentic 3D modeling framework that leverages the code generation ability of an LLM and scales it to 3D shapes with high-grade detail and native, meaningful part decomposition. Specifically, Procedura lets frozen LLM write the shape in constructive solid geometry (CSG), where every face is an exact plane or cylinder, so edges come out sharp where generated mesh stays soft. Our key idea is to cast the code as procedural assembly, parametric program whose named parts are joined by typed, machine-checkable mates such as peg into socket or hinge about an axis. This structure turns one large blind generation into many small, checkable steps. Every part is named, editable module  (Fig. 2)  that the model writes in single call, each placement is solved from the mated frames rather than guessed, and compile, mate, and connectivity checks admit every commit, so the build grows into detailed, many-part object without drifting [48]. Given text prompt, Procedura synthesizes reference view, plans the assembly graph, builds the program part by part, and refines it with decoupled vision critic  (Fig. 3)  . We evaluate Procedura on P3D-Bench under its assembly judge, and with the same judge on MechBench-36, our hard-surface benchmark, against native generators, prior 3D-code agents, and single-shot LLM baselines. On both benchmarks, Procedura outperforms all of them on judged quality. Our contributions are as follows: 3D-shape-as-code modeling agent. We explore the paradigm of 3D shape as code and introduce Procedura, an agentic framework that leverages and scales the coding ability of frozen LLM for 3D modeling, yielding detailed, many-part 3D shapes from text prompt with no 3D training. Procedural assembly with typed mates. We represent an object as parametric CSG program whose named parts are joined by typed, machine-checkable mates. Placement is solved from the mated frames and every commit is verified, so the build stays connected and precise and every part remains editable by name. The same graph further carries per-part materials and simulator-validated articulation. Benchmark and state-of-the-art results. On P3D-Bench and on MechBench-36, Procedura outperforms state-of-the-art native 3D generators and all prior 3D-code agents, with the sharpest edges and the only editable, part-structured output.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Native 3D generation. large body of work synthesizes 3D shape directly as continuous geometry. Optimization-based methods distill 2D diffusion prior through score distillation [23, 30, 38], reaching high fidelity at the cost of long per-object optimization. Feed-forward methods map prompt or single image to point cloud, an implicit field, or set of Gaussians in one pass [11, 18, 28, 36, 54], and native 3D diffusion models now recover mesh geometry of striking fidelity and broad coverage [15, 37, 42, 43, 46]. In parallel, autoregressive models emit the mesh itself token by token [5, 27, 35]. However, these models optimize fidelity to the input view alone. Trained on scanned and artist-made surfaces, they emit dense, soft, scan-like meshes with no named parts, no editable dimensions, and rounded edges where machined object needs sharp ones. Part structure, when needed, comes from post-hoc segmentation model [24, 50, 51], which cuts the surface after the fact and attaches no dimensions or relations to the parts it names. In contrast, we represent an object as the assembly program that constructs it, which makes parts, dimensions, and relations explicit while requiring no 3D training. Program-based 3D generation. Representing shape as the program that builds it yields an inherently editable, parametric model. Early work induces constructive solid geometry (CSG) trees [19, 32] or structured assembly programs [17], and CAD-native methods learn sketch-extrude command sequences from large engineering datasets [40, 41, 47]. More recently, large language models write parametric 3D programs directly or translate text into construction-command sequences [20, 26]; semantic commenting then recovers part labels for an existing program [53]. Production CAD treats assembly itself as first-class object, where graph of typed mates between part-local connectors drives placement and kinematics alike, and design-forassembly practice prescribes how good parts join: self-locating features, matched malefemale pairs sharing one nominal dimension, and explicit fits [4]. Learned-assembly research brings that structure to machine learning, predicting mates or joints for existing human-made parts [16, 39] from large CAD datasets. However, no generative system authors this structure. The program-writing line remains single-shot, producing the code once with no visual feedback, so many-part objects come out with wrong part counts and misplaced parts [48], and nothing in the emitted program states how two parts relate. Procedura generates the parts and their mate graph jointly, building part by part against render of what is already placed, so the structure that assembly research assumes as input becomes our output. Agentic 3D-code generation. Closest to our setting, recent systems wrap general LLM in draft-executerevise loop that writes 3D code, runs the compiler, and revises from rendered or programmatic feedback [1, 3, 7, 34, 55], and domain-tuned coders fine-tune model to emit CAD code [10, 21]. Beyond static shape, agentic pipelines author articulated assets by generating code for parts and their kinematics [34, 55], visionlanguage systems articulate an existing mesh by predicting its joints [22], and LLM scene systems arrange retrieved assets by predicted layout or sample procedural environments [6, 8, 12, 31, 49]. These systems confirm that coding agent can turn prompt into an editable program, yet they share two limits. Parts are glued by raw transforms the model estimates from picture, and kinematics is stage that follows geometry, so joint axis is fitted to finished surface rather than read off the structure that placed the part. Procedura answers both. Every relation is typed mate checked on the compiled mesh, so placement is solved rather than guessed and connectivity is enforced during generation instead of patched afterward [2, 14]; kinematic mates live in the same graph, so hinge is the very relation that seated its two parts. Moreover, an independent vision critic, separate from the model that wrote the code, diagnoses every build and gates each edit. Selfrefinement instead lets the same model critique its own output [25, 33, 52], and such reviewer often fails to find its own errors [13]. 4 Figure 4. The mate library. The nine static mating features part may declare, each rendered from the compiler macros the build emits. Teal is the male half added to the new part and grey the female half cut from its partner; both derive from one shared nominal dimension and signed fit offset.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Given text prompt, our goal is 3D model that meets the three requirements of Sec. 1: high-precision geometry, meaningful part decomposition, and editability. Procedura therefore generates the program that builds the mesh rather than the mesh itself. We define this representation, procedural assembly whose parts are joined by typed mates (Sec. 3.1). The agent authors it in three stages  (Fig. 3)  : it plans the assembly graph (Sec. 3.2), builds the program one part at time under solved placement and deterministic verification (Sec. 3.3), and refines it through decoupled vision critic (Sec. 3.4). The same graph also completes the asset with per-part materials (Sec. 3.5) and simulator-validated articulation (Sec. 3.6). One frozen LLM drives every reasoning step, so Procedura needs no 3D training; every other component in the pipeline is deterministic. 3.1 Procedural Assembly Representation Formulation. Procedura represents an object as procedural assembly 𝐴 = (𝑃, 𝐶), where 𝑃 = {𝑝1, , 𝑝𝑛} is an ordered set of parts, each named parametric CSG module, and 𝐶 is set of mates, each typed relation between the mate frames of two parts. The shipped geometry is the mesh 𝑀 = COMPILE(𝐴) that the compiler produces. This representation answers the three requirements by construction. Geometry is precise since programs faces are planes and its bores are cylinders, so its edges stay sharp at any resolution. The part decomposition is the module list itself, so it is exact and needs no separate segmentation model. Editing is parameter change, since every dimension is named parameter bound to named part. The representation also records relations. mate states how two parts join, so placement can be solved and verified, and the same relation later drives articulation. Typed mates. mate 𝑐 = (𝑖, 𝑗, type, 𝐹𝑖, 𝐹𝑗, 𝑑, 𝜙) joins frame 𝐹𝑗 published by the new part 𝑝𝑗 to frame 𝐹𝑖 published by an earlier part 𝑝𝑖. Its type is drawn from closed vocabulary of nine static mating features (bolt-pattern, peg-socket, seat-face, flange, tab-slot, press-fit, lip-rabbet, snap-tab, and key; Fig. 4) and three kinematic ones (revolute, prismatic, and spherical). The two halves share one nominal dimension 𝑑, and fit class 𝜙 {clearance, location, press, snap} resolves to signed per-side offset in millimetres. Two rules follow. First, both halves of mate derive from the same parameter 𝑑 plus signed fit offset, never from two literals, so an edit to one side can never orphan the other. Second, each type fixes degree-of-freedom signature, so static mate fully locates its part while kinematic mate leaves exactly the intended motion free.

sections.title: 3.2 Assembly-Graph Planning
sections.content: Part plan with mates. Given the prompt, Procedura first synthesizes single reference view, which grounds every later stage. single vision call then decomposes the object into an ordered list of named 5 Figure 5. Mate-driven building. Top: for each planned part, the dynamic context packs three grounded sources into one generation message: (a) the assembly reference, namely the reference image, the prompt, and the parts mate, shown here beside the verdict its mesh check returned; (b) the built history, the full and already-compiling program; and (c) 3D feedback, parts-colour renders of the build so far. Bottom: the program grows one part per mate, shown as five snapshots of the assault buggy at 2, 10, 18, 24, and 28 parts. Each part is generated in one LLM call and parsed into five blocks. The splice is deterministic and the placement is solved from the mated frames, and the compile, mate, and span gates must all pass before the part is committed. Every commit re-renders the 3D feedback for the next part. parts. Each part carries snake_case module name, coarse detail level (silhouette, major feature, or subfeature), and short description that fixes its relative size, aspect, and pose against its neighbours. Each part also carries its interface declarations, the typed mates that bind it to parts placed earlier, each naming the partner, the mate type, and the shared nominal. The list is ordered so that every part attaches to one placed earlier. It is therefore topological order of the assembly graph, which lets the build seat each module on geometry that already exists. Mirror pairs, such as left and right arm, are kept as separate parts, since hand-assembled object is rarely perfectly symmetric and later stages edit each side independently. One-direction plan review. second vision call reviews the plan against the reference, and we allow it to revise in only one direction. It may add missing part or sharpen description or mate, but it may never merge, remove, rename, or reorder. The rule matters because each part is exactly one generation call in the build, so merging two parts into one removes detail the builder would otherwise produce. We enforce it in code instead of trusting the prompt, so every original part survives with its name and position, and only genuinely new part is admitted, inserted after the part it attaches to. The reviewed graph is the plan the build consumes.

sections.title: 3.3 Mate-Driven Building
sections.content: One part per call. single LLM call can write the whole program for simple shape. However, detailed, many-part object forces that one call to fix every part, count, and placement at once, and the model loses track, leaving misplaced sub-assemblies and floaters. To address this, the build grows the program one module at time, in plan order, so each call solves the small problem of adding single part to model that already exists. The call emits only the new part, in strict five-block format: new parameters, helper modules, the part body, its published interface frames, and its placement intent. simpler one-shot mode, which writes the entire program in single call, is the control our experiments compare against (Sec. 4). 6 Dynamic context. Each generation call sees three grounded sources  (Fig. 5)  . The assembly reference is the reference image, the text prompt, and the plan slice, namely the part to add, its mates, the parts not yet built, and mandate to match the references relative size, aspect, and pose. The built history is the full accumulated program, passed as text; because it already compiles, the model reads exact parameters and frames instead of guessing the current scale. The 3D feedback is parts-colour render of the build from up to twelve viewpoints, six orthographic faces and six isometric corners. Each committed part carries distinct colour, so the model can see where its part attaches. The first part, with nothing yet built, receives the reference and plan alone. Solved placement. The model authors the parts geometry and its mate frames but not the assembly transform. For static mate joining the new parts frame 𝐹𝑗 to the placed partner frame 𝐹𝑖, the placement is the rigid transform that aligns them: 𝑇𝑗 = 𝐹𝑖 Δ(𝜙) 𝐹1 where Δ(𝜙) denotes the signed fit offset along the mate axis. Solving 𝑇𝑗 in code removes the largest single source of drift in prior 3D-code systems, since the model never emits raw transform it estimated from render. part with several static mates is placed by the first and checked against the rest. (1) , 𝑗 Deterministic splice. The five blocks are spliced into the accumulating program at fixed marker comments. Parameters are appended and de-duplicated, module whose name collides is renamed, and the solved placement is inserted into the assembly. The LLM authors only the new part, so the program grows without the generator ever re-emitting or corrupting what earlier calls produced. Verification stack. spliced part must clear three deterministic checks before it joins the build. First, compile gate compiles the program; on failure the compilers error text is fed back and the part is regenerated. Second, mate gate measures each of the parts static mates on the compiled mesh, testing the registration area 𝑎(𝑐) of the mated surfaces and the penetration depth 𝛿(𝑐) between the two bodies: 𝑎(𝑐) 𝜏𝑎 𝑑2 and 𝛿(𝑐) 𝛿max(𝜙), (2) where 𝑑 denotes the mates nominal and 𝛿max the tolerance its fit class allows. part that merely hovers near its partner, or gouges into it, is therefore rejected, with the measured values returned in the feedback. Third, delta-aware connectivity gate reuses the span measure of Sec. 3.4 and rejects the part only when it increases the count of visible floaters over the running baseline, so part that legitimately connects late is never blocked. Each part gets up to three quality attempts. When it exhausts them it is committed with warning rather than dropped, since completion matters more than defect the refine loop can still remove; part that never compiles is skipped. When the plan is exhausted, the markers are stripped, yielding the draft assembly the refine loop takes up.

sections.title: 3.4 Decoupled-Critic Refinement
sections.content: The draft assembly is complete but imperfect, so refine loop polishes it. Each cycle renders the current build, has critic diagnose it against the reference, and applies the top defect, followed by verify compile. The defining choice is to decouple the critic from the fixer, so the agent repairs what separate reviewer reports rather than what it judges of its own work. Decoupled critic. The reviewer is separate, single-turn vision call. It runs the same underlying model with its own system prompt and context, never as turn of the agent that writes code. It sees the reference, the views the agent just rendered, the parts-colour legend, and the current program, and returns one-line SUMMARY and prioritized ISSUES list, each issue tagged [HIGHMEDLOW] and naming the responsible module with one-sentence fix direction. We decouple the two for three reasons. First, model that judges its own 7 output carries the very assumptions that produced the error, so an independent reviewer is more likely to catch it. Second, the diagnosis becomes persisted, first-class artifact, whereas in freeform loop the critique lives only in hidden reasoning. Third, the critic is history-aware, receiving trail of what prior cycles flagged, so it verifies that earlier fixes landed and flags regressions  (Fig. 11)  . Diagnosis-gated edits. The ordering is hard invariant, enforced in code. successful diagnose sets one-shot latch that exactly one subsequent edit consumes. The edit tools refuse unless the latch is set, and diagnose itself refuses if the rendered views are stale with respect to the current program. Without the gate the agent edits repeatedly off stale review; an ungated variant issued 15 edits against 2 diagnoses, whereas the gated loop holds the diagnose-to-edit ratio at 1 1. Agent-chosen context. The agent selects which views to render and how many (1 to 20) from fixed catalog of orthographic faces, isometric corners, eye-level diagonals, and front tilts. On fresh model it surveys broadly so no side hides defect; once problem is localized it renders the focused subset that best shows it. refine step is bounded by single module edit, and only edits count against the budget. After the edit, the agent compiles and, when the compile flags floaters, checks connectivity within the same cycle, so broken edit is caught before it wastes the next review. The agent ends with ok when the critic reports no HIGH issue, or give_up when several edits fail to shrink the issue list. Figure 6. sections.title: 3.5 Materials
sections.content: Material library and assignment. Geometry alone does not make production asset, so the same graph also carries material for every part. Paint runs once the geometry is frozen and changes only colour and surface; the whole stage is four one-shot vision calls with no agent loop. Procedura first reads the reference image and catalogues every distinct surface as compact material library, typically one to two dozen physically-based-rendering (PBR) entries with albedo, class, roughness, metalness, and wear. It then assigns one library material to each named part, so the palette is grounded in the reference and shared across parts made of the same thing. As with geometry, separate vision critic compares render of the painted model to the reference and returns corrected assignment. Sub-part colour blocks. One material per module is often too coarse, since one wheel module carries rubber tread, painted rim, and cast hub. Procedura therefore rewrites module into sibling colour blocks so sub-feature takes its own material, recompiling each rewrite and rejecting any whose triangle count moves beyond fixed tolerance, so colour can never alter the shape. The stage emits colour-tagged program, multi-group OBJ+MTL with per-part PBR fields, and Blender-Cycles studio render  (Fig. 7)  ; every artifact stays parts-addressable.

sections.title: 3.6 Articulation
sections.content: Turning the same parts into jointed, physically validated asset requires no new structure, since the mate network is already the kinematic graph. Static mates group parts into rigid links. Each kinematic mate, whether revolute, prismatic, or spherical, names its joint, axis, and anchor, and is either authored at plan time or promoted later from geometric evidence. Geometric evidence. Procedura measures the geometry before any reasoning about motion. For each part it computes two kinds of evidence: rotational-symmetry axes, taken from the area-weighted covariance of the parts surface triangles, and contact regions between touching parts. Both are deterministic and yield concrete axis and anchor candidates, so wheels spin axis or hinge line starts from measured geometry. Joint planning and validation. vision call then completes the articulation. It groups modules into links, 9 Figure 8. sim-ready articulation validated in Isaac Sim. From the rovers named parts, Procedura measures geometric evidence (the rotational-symmetry axes and contact regions) and plans the joint tree over the kinematic mates (17 links, 16 joints). It exports an OpenUSD articulation and URDF and validates them headless in Isaac Sim; failed verdict feeds rendered simulation frames back to the planner for one refine. Every panel is real Isaac frame in per-link colours: the settled rest pose, four per-joint actuation sweeps, and the rover after nine-wheel drive. builds the parentchild tree over the kinematic mates, and assigns each joint its axes, limits, and drives. The plan is refined against deterministic feedback and exported as an OpenUSD articulation and URDF, so the same object drops into physics simulator or robotics stack. Procedura then validates the plan headless in Isaac Sim through fixed battery: dynamic settle, per-joint actuation sweeps, rest-contact scan, wheeled mobility test, and URDF re-import. flagged fault feeds up to eight rendered simulation frames back to the planner for one refine, so the critic can see wrong axis  (Fig. 8)  .

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Our experiments answer three questions. Does mate-driven shape-as-code make frozen LLM state-ofthe-art 3D generator, measured against native generators, prior 3D-code agents, and single-shot prompting of the same models (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3)? What do the pipelines stages contribute (Sec. 4.4)? And does the program deliver what mesh cannot, namely full production asset (Sec. 4.5)? Throughout we report intervals and paired tests rather than single numbers.

sections.title: 4.1 Setup and Protocol
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on two benchmarks. The first is MechBench-36, our hard-surface benchmark, frozen set of 36 deliberately many-part objects, rovers, mechs, cranes, excavators, engines, and landing gear, chosen because they stress part counts, placement, and connectivity far harder than single-sub-assembly shape (Sec. 4.2). The second is the assembly task of P3D-Bench [48], 203 text-and-image cases scored by the benchmarks own assembly judge (Sec. 4.3). Procedura normally synthesizes its own reference view from the prompt; for evaluation we lock both the prompt and that view and hand the same pair to every method, so image synthesis cannot confound the comparison. Blind judging protocol. Judging generated 3D by eye invites bias, so the protocol removes each confound in turn. sections.title: 4.2 Results on MechBench-36
sections.content: MechBench-36 concentrates the many-part regime that motivates Procedura. As shown in Tab. 1, Procedura takes the top judge composite at 0.828 with Gemini 3.7 Flash, leads geometry, aesthetics, and CLIP, and ships mesh for every case. TRELLIS.2 follows at 0.810; Adam CAD at 0.799 and our GPT-5.6-sol arm at 0.797 are effectively tied. 11 Axis-level analysis. The judges axes do not separate the field equally. Semantic spans only 0.775 to 0.861 across the methods that work at all, since that axis mostly asks whether the object is of the right kind; Adam CAD and TRELLIS.2 share its top at 0.861, whisker above our 0.858. Geometry and aesthetics separate the methods far more, spanning 0.583 to 0.799 and 0.105 to 0.827, and Procedura tops both. Comparison with native generators. Native generators map an image to dense surface whose creases come out rounded. The strongest of them, TRELLIS.2, trails by 5.2 CLIP points, and Direct3D-S2 and Hunyuan3D fall behind on aesthetics by 0.27 and 0.24. In Fig. 10, the natives reproduce the silhouette faithfully but blur bolt heads, vents, and panel lines into the surrounding body, whereas our compiled CSG keeps every feature crisp and every part separable. Comparison with prior 3D-code agents. The strongest prior agent, Adam CAD on GPT-5.6-sol, reaches 0.759 aesthetics and 81.26 CLIP. The domain-tuned coders CAD-Coder and cadrille collapse on many-part objects, scoring 0.210 and 0.105 and shipping no mesh on 1 and 5 cases, since model trained to emit one sketch-extrude body cannot express an assembly. The same failure is visible in Fig. 9, where the prior agents keep the outline of each machine but simplify its mechanism into few large blocks. Edge structure. The two right-hand columns measure the edge structure each representation produces, and Procedura leads both. Our programs carry 158.1 units of sharp edge above 60 dihedral with Gemini 3.7 Flash and 185.2 with GPT-5.6-sol, 2.6 and 3.1 the next code-emitting method, at 95th-percentile dihedrals of 98.0 and 105.3. The native generators sit at 3373, since surface regressed from samples has no notion of face or bore. TRELLIS.2 posts the only comparable sharp-edge length at 134.0, yet its 73.1 dihedral shows those creases are far shallower than ours. The gap follows from the representation, since an edge in compiled CSG is the exact intersection of two analytic surfaces. Paired gain over the base model. Every row uses frozen model, so the pipeline can be ablated against single call to the same model on the same case. Paired per object over the whole benchmark, the pipeline improves aesthetics by +0.105 on Gemini 3.7 Flash (20 wins, 7 losses, sign test 𝑝 = 0.019); on GPT-5.6-sol the mean gain is +0.059 but the split is 15 wins to 11 losses (𝑝 = 0.56), so we do not claim significance there. CLIP improves by +1.80 (𝑝 = 0.011) and +0.85 respectively. The gain concentrates on aesthetics, the axis the mate-driven build targets.

sections.content: P3D-Benchs judge scores each case on the three axes of Sec. 4.1, and its composite is the mean of the three after normalization. We re-render and re-judge every method under the shared harness, so every row of Tab. 2 is directly comparable. As shown in Tab. 2, Procedura solves all 203 cases with either base model and leads every column. The composite reaches 0.590 on Gemini 3.7 Flash and 0.575 on GPT-5.6-sol, against 0.524 for the strongest entry that also covers the full benchmark, margin several times the 95% intervals. Notably, the lead is largest on geometry, 0.490 against 0.392, which is exactly where the mate-driven build acts, since solved placement and verified connectivity are geometric properties. Gain over single-shot prompting. Prompting our two base models once reaches 0.566 and 0.563 on the reduced sets those runs cover, above every published entry, so one call to frontier model already clears the published leaderboard. Part of any margin over the published rows therefore reflects base-model strength rather than method; the agent supplies the remaining margin. per-case paired comparison puts the full pipeline above the Gemini 3.7 Flash control on the cases it covers, and the pipeline also solves the cases the control does not. 12 Procedura (ours) GPT-5.6 (img) Gemini 3.1 Pro (img) Adam CAD ArtiCraft six-wheeled Mars rover with boxy chassis, an articulated camera mast, and broad flat solar-panel wings. Every removal costs quality on every column, and the full pipeline is the best variant on all five. Dropping the refine loop lowers the composite from 0.828 to 0.800, the cleanest read of what the decoupled critics gated edits add, since that variant differs from the full pipeline by refine alone. It reports the front winch 1.25 road-tire diameter ahead of the front axle against roughly 0.60.7 in the reference, and gun receiver at 0.19 the tire diameter against 0.300.35, and the agent answers each with single tool call on the named modules. sections.title: 4.5 Materials and Articulation
sections.content: Materials. Because every part is named module, physically-based material is per-part attribute the program simply carries. Fig. 7 shows an object painted from its reference alone, where the extract, assign, critic, and sub-part passes recover distinct metals, rubber, and glass, and Fig. 13 shows the same stage across the benchmark. We report no paint metric, since there is no ground-truth material map and colour distance against generated reference would score the reference rather than the model. Articulation. Articulation, in contrast, can be checked objectively, since the physics simulator is an independent oracle. Across the 18 objects we have articulated and validated, 14 clear every dynamics phase settle, per-joint actuation, rest-contact scan, and URDF re-import and 9 of those also clear the advisory asset rules; the four that fail outright are one asset that would not load and three whose actuators never traverse  (Fig. 12)  . 16 Figure 13. Texturing across the benchmark. Ten of the 36 benchmark objects, geometry and materials both authored by Procedura. Every image is Blender-Cycles render of the shipped program, with per-part materials assigned to the named modules.

sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: Procedura produces editable procedural assemblies that surpass native generators on judged quality, yet three limitations remain. First, the agent perceives the build only through rendered images. rendered view conveys silhouette and placement well, but occluded interiors and fine contact geometry can hide from every camera; depth maps, cross-sections, or direct mesh queries would strengthen the loop. Second, CSG captures mechanical, hard-surface objects precisely, whereas organic, freeform surfaces are expressed less naturally than in neural field. Third, the mate vocabulary covers rigid joints only, and mate the plan never declares cannot be verified.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Procedura, procedural assembly agent that generates 3D object as the program that builds it, parametric assembly whose named parts are joined by typed, machine-checkable mates. frozen LLM authors this representation with no 3D training, planning the assembly graph, building the program part by part with placement solved from the mated frames and every commit verified, and refining the result through decoupled vision critic. The same graph then carries per-part materials and simulator-validated articulation. On P3D-Bench and on MechBench-36, judged blind, Procedura leads every native generator and prior 3D-code agent on judged quality, carries the sharpest edges of any method we measure, and is the only system whose output re-opens as an editable, part-structured program. Its principles carry to programbased generation at large: casting shape generation as coding, joining parts by verifiable mates, separating the critic from the fixer, and validating every claim in compiler or simulator.
